dateLabel: 5 Nov comparison completed · 3 Nov follow-up · 1 Nov readiness review
summary: The controlled outlet comparison is complete. Matching-time histories show a coherent computed late-load difference, mainly through pressure, while pitch-moment drift remains unresolved. The final interpretation is inconclusive. H0 is unchanged and free heave/pitch release remains on hold.
evidence: Completed numerical sensitivity experiment · interpretation inconclusive · no physical validation
changes: 5 November completed outlet-comparison follow-up, with final matched-window evidence and independent engineering review. The 3 November experiment-start account and 1 November fixed-baseline readiness hold remain dated history. Numerical completion does not establish outlet causation, a preferred replacement baseline, validated drag, stable trim or permission to change H0. No further CFD follows automatically.

sections.title: 5 November 2026: the comparison is complete
sections.text:
The bounded outlet experiment has reached its accepted one-second endpoint, and the final engineering review is complete. It tested whether changing the downstream velocity treatment affected the fixed-hull calculation. The two branches shared a saved starting state and were compared over matching simulation-time intervals. Hull geometry, pose, speed and mesh stayed the same; heave and pitch remained locked.

The completed records show a coherent computed late-load difference. In the final window, upward fluid force rose from about 183 to 217 N and positive bow-up moment from about 400 to 407 N·m. Pressure supplied about 95% of that moment difference. These are finite-duration numerical findings on a restrained hull. They do not establish measured board performance or make the alternative outlet a physically validated replacement.

sections.title: A load offset did not cure the drift
sections.text:
The distinction between load level and load development matters. The alternative branch carried a higher mean bow-up moment in both late windows. Yet the change from the penultimate to final window remained almost the same: approximately −6.18 N·m for the original branch and −6.12 N·m for the alternative. The latter still exceeded the unchanged preparation criterion.

Moving the comparison windows earlier changed the estimated migration contrast, including its sign. The experiment therefore does not establish that the alternative treatment removed the drift or that the branches are equivalent. Neither a smaller fitted slope nor a single endpoint value can settle that question. The fixed-preparation readiness finding remains on hold.

figure.alt: Paired bars show W3 minus W2 mean bow-up moment: baseline A minus 6.179586 newton metres and alternative B minus 6.118881 newton metres. Both retain similar nominal late migration.
figure.caption: Migration is the difference between two time-weighted interval means, W3 minus W2, not an instantaneous rate or a fitted slope. W2 spans 0.579867–0.789933 s; W3 spans 0.789933–1.000000 s. The nominal contrast is only +0.060705 N·m, but earlier shifted-window choices change its sign. This does not establish a drift cure or equivalence.

sections.title: An inconclusive result still changes what we know
sections.text:
Splitting the final window into four equal parts exposes substantial transient structure: the moment difference alternates sign, even though the complete-window average is positive. These shorter intervals do not cancel the full-window finding or form independent statistical samples.

The final classification is inconclusive. The computed late-load response is supported, while general data and restart qualification, history-wide phase interpretation and persistent matched spatial evidence remain incomplete. A single nominal endpoint pressure comparison adds useful spatial context; it cannot establish sustained causation or prove a returning reflection.

The completed experiment is preserved for the next engineering decision. It does not select a new baseline. H0 and its source geometry remain unchanged, heave and pitch remain locked, and no further CFD follows automatically. Physical validation and any decision about free motion remain ahead.

figure.alt: Four signed bars show alternative B minus baseline A bow-up moment means across equal quarters of W3: positive 36.02, negative 20.92, positive 16.68 and negative 2.79 newton metres. The complete W3 mean difference is positive 7.25 newton metres.
figure.caption: Four equal subdivisions of W3, 0.789933–1.000000 s, give time-weighted B−A bow-up moment differences of +36.016635, −20.915394, +16.684589 and −2.790897 N·m. Their average is the complete W3 difference, +7.248733 N·m. The quarter values reveal transient phase structure; they are not independent samples, uncertainty bounds or evidence that the full-window response disappears.

sections.title: Follow-up · 3 November 2026: test the boundary before changing the hull
sections.text:
The 1 November review left an important question open: why was the pitching moment still evolving while H0, Wahoo's developing hull, remained fixed? The outlet is the downstream edge of the simulated water domain. How flow leaves that edge could influence the calculation, but the earlier evidence did not establish that it caused the observed behaviour.

On 2 November, a new, bounded experiment was authorized to test sensitivity to the outlet velocity treatment. That authorization is a separate step after the earlier diagnostic hold; it does not overturn the readiness finding or authorize changes to H0. The original baseline remains preserved, and vertical motion (heave) and fore-aft rotation (pitch) remain locked. Testing the numerical boundary first helps avoid changing the hull in response to an unresolved numerical effect.

The load histories below are retained fixed-baseline evidence from the 1 November review, not results from this new comparison.

sections.title: 3 November method record · two branches, the same simulation clock
sections.text:
The comparison reuses the original baseline and starts a separate test branch from exactly the same saved flow state. Only the outlet velocity treatment changes. Hull geometry, pose, speed, mesh and the other numerical settings stay the same.

The comparison requires matching intervals of physical simulation time, using saved samples covering those same intervals. Comparing a later test interval with an earlier baseline interval could confuse ordinary flow development with a boundary effect. The shared starting state and equal-time comparison address that problem.

A dated 3 November record confirms that the test resumed and advanced after recovery. This records the start and resumption of an experiment; its comparison result has not yet been accepted. The evidence reviewed here does not yet establish whether the outlet treatment materially changes the loads or pitching moment. No new drag, stability or physical-performance claim follows.

figure.alt: Transparent method-only diagram: the same saved initial state branches to preserved baseline A and an alternative outlet velocity treatment B. Comparison requires matching physical-time intervals. H0 is unchanged, heave and pitch locked, comparative result pending.
figure.caption: A controlled comparison changes one outlet velocity treatment. This is an explanatory method diagram, not a CFD contour, force history or accepted comparison result.

sections.title: Readiness review · 1 November 2026: numerical completion, readiness held
sections.text:
The controlled 30 km/h preparation run has reached its nominal one-second checkpoint. The solver exited normally, and an independent check accepted the saved numerical state. That is a useful milestone for H0, Wahoo's developing hull. It does not mean the flow is ready for the next experiment.

The current H0 dry-hull baseline remained fixed in its original pose throughout this stage. H0 geometry and the Rhino source remain unchanged. Vertical motion, or heave, and fore-aft rotation, or pitch, stayed locked. We have not released those motions or demonstrated stable trim. The purpose was to prepare and examine the flow before asking how the hull would respond.

figure.alt: Retained 1 November fixed-baseline numerical load histories, not outlet A/B results. Drag, upward force and bow-up moment about CG.
figure.caption: 1 November baseline evidence, preserved: numerical histories approximately 0.370–1.000 s. Cyan recorded loads; dashed time-weighted window means. Every fiftieth native sample displayed, all samples used for statistics. Bow-up = −My about the accepted CG. No smoothing or physical validation. This is not the 5 November outlet comparison.

sections.title: One question at a time
sections.text:
Earlier work included a transition from 20 to 30 km/h. A speed ramp changes the conditions while the flow is developing. It can be useful in a commissioning sequence, but it makes the subsequent evidence harder to interpret: a changing load may reflect the changing imposed speed, continuing flow development, or both.

The controlled experiment holds the imposed speed at 30 km/h and holds the hull's pose. That narrows the question. Before allowing heave and pitch, is the prepared flow sufficiently repeatable under the agreed readiness checks? A fixed body is a deliberate experimental condition, not a substitute for a freely responding board.

The nominal one-second endpoint is simulation time. It is not a physical test, a rider trial or a statement about how long a real board takes to settle.

sections.title: The solver finished. The engineering did not.
sections.text:
A complete checkpoint answers a numerical question: did the run reach its endpoint and leave a usable saved state? Readiness asks a different question: does the evolving flow support the next stage of the experiment?

The recorded histories were compared over three late windows, each approximately one hull-length transit time at the imposed speed. Drag and vertical-fluid-force averages became more repeatable between the final two windows. Their instantaneous loads still fluctuated. A small change in an average should not be mistaken for quiet flow, a fully stationary result or validated drag.

Pitch moment gives a more cautious answer. Its three window means continued to change. The final adjacent change remained beyond the preparation criterion, even though late fluctuation repeatability improved. The full set of readiness checks was therefore not satisfied.

That finding concerns preparation of this numerical experiment. A nonzero moment on a restrained hull does not, by itself, establish instability, a hull defect or a stable running attitude. Those conclusions would require different evidence.

sections.title: Why we did not release the board
sections.text:
We retained the accepted checkpoint and kept heave and pitch locked. Numerical completion did not earn automatic progression.

Review of the saved evidence shows continuing redistribution of pressure and contact proxies, along with evolving downstream flow. These observations make the next question more specific, but they do not resolve its cause. Ordinary settling, persistent unsteadiness and possible outlet or boundary influence have not been separated causally.

The diagnostic conclusion is inconclusive. That does not reverse the readiness finding: the preparation is not ready for release. Nor does it prove that reflected waves returned from the outlet, that one boundary condition caused the drift, or that a longer run would cure it. The available evidence does not yet justify prescribing extra CFD duration or a boundary change.

sections.title: Evidence before speed
sections.text:
Archimedes's next technical question is which existing evidence can distinguish continued development from a material domain or boundary effect. Leo's integration question is what decision that evidence would enable, and whether any further computation would be justified. A hull change should follow a supported engineering diagnosis, rather than an attempt to make an inconvenient trace disappear.

The working principle is simple: do not force the answer you want. When the evidence is not ready, stop and investigate. This milestone is progress because it gives us a checked checkpoint and a clear reason to hold the next stage. Physical validation and performance claims remain ahead.
